transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me?

Well, I'm here because everybody keeps acting like I’m just imagining it. But I know my wife’s relative came into this house to get at me. I mean, my tools don’t move themselves. I work as an assembler, fabricating parts, so I know exactly where my gear is at all times. You have to on the line, otherwise you get backed up. My supervisor, Dave, he's always on us about a clean station, which makes sense because last month this new kid left a torque wrench out and... well, anyway. 

My tools at home. They're being moved. And my fishing plans get spoiled every single weekend, and it’s not an accident. I love fishing for bass. You ever go? If you use a green spinnerbait right at dawn, they just hammer it. I got this new tackle box for my birthday, the kind with the fold-out trays... but yeah, after all these months of this going on, I can see it plain as day. He’s been trying to take over my place and push me out.
Have you been using any alcohol, marijuana, stimulants, or other drugs recently, or at any point around when these experiences started?

Drugs? No, no way. I don't touch any of that. No pills, no weed, nothing. You can't be messing with that stuff when you work the line anyway, they do random screenings. Dave, my supervisor, he actually had to let a guy go a couple years back because he popped for something on a test. Real shame, too, because the guy was a heck of a welder. 

He actually showed me this trick with TIG welding aluminum where you kind of pulse the foot pedal just right to get that perfect stack-of-dimes look on the bead. It's an art, really. Most of these new kids coming in, they just want to use the MIG spool gun because it's faster, but it looks so sloppy. You ever do any welding? It's tough on the eyes if you don't have a good auto-darkening hood. I bought this really nice one, a Lincoln, cost me a pretty penny. I used to keep it out in the garage on my workbench, but... well, I can't leave it out there anymore. Not with him coming around and putting his hands on my things. But yeah, no drugs or anything like that.
How long has it been since you first started noticing that your tools were being moved and that your wife's relative was involved?

Well, it's been about nine months now. Yeah, right around nine months. That's when he moved in with us. We had that spare room, you know, the one I used to use for my model trains. I had an O-gauge setup in there, took up half the room. I spent three winters building the mountain scenery out of foam board and plaster. You have to get the plaster just right, kind of soupy, or it dries too fast and you can't carve the rock faces. I used to paint them with these washes, layered them up—burnt umber, raw sienna—to make it look like real granite. It looked incredible, especially when the little streetlamps lit up. My grandson loved it. He'd sit there for hours watching the Santa Fe Chief go around. But we had to pack it all up in boxes when he needed a place to stay. Now those boxes are just sitting in the basement collecting dust, and who knows if the tracks are even getting bent. Anyway, ever since he moved into that room, that's when all this started. Nine months of my life, just... turned upside down.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you don't seem to notice or hear?

Voices? No, nothing like that. I don't hear things that aren't there. My hearing is actually pretty good, considering the noise on the floor at work. We wear those foam earplugs, you know, the orange ones you roll up and stick in your ear? You gotta roll 'em real tight, otherwise they just pop right back out before they seat properly. A lot of guys don't wear 'em right, and then they wonder why their ears ring at the end of the shift. The stamping press alone is like... well, it's loud. Thump. Thump. Thump. All day. You can feel it in your boots. I buy my own boots, Red Wings, steel toe. The company gives us a voucher for fifty bucks, but that doesn't even cover half a good pair. You gotta take care of your feet if you're standing on concrete for eight hours. My buddy Stan, he tried to cheap out on boots once and ended up with plantar fasciitis. Kept him out of work for a month. But yeah, my hearing is fine, I don't hear any weird voices or anything.
Have you had any recent or past medical problems—like a head injury, seizures, thyroid issues, or other illnesses—that a doctor has diagnosed or treated you for?

Medical problems? No, no, nothing like that. My health is fine. I haven't had any head injuries or seizures or anything. I did get a pretty nasty cut on my forearm once, though, back when I was working at the old sheet metal shop over on 4th Street. That place was a real hazard, let me tell you. The brake press they had was from the 1960s, didn't have any of the safety guards they require nowadays. You had to really watch your fingers. 

Anyway, I was trying to muscle a piece of 14-gauge stainless into the shear, and the edge caught me right above the glove line. Bled like a stuck pig. Had to go to the urgent care and get seven stitches. The doctor there, young guy, looked like he was fresh out of school, he did a real nice job sewing it up, though. Barely even a scar now. You have to be so careful with stainless, the edges are like razors when they come off the cutter. I always tell the new guys, wear your Kevlar sleeves. They complain that they're hot and itchy, especially in the summer when the shop gets up to ninety degrees, but I'd rather be sweating than bleeding, you know? But yeah, no major medical issues or anything. I'm pretty healthy.
Aside from these concerns about your wife's relative, have you noticed any changes in how you're doing at work, socially, or in taking care of yourself day-to-day over these past nine months?

Changes? No. I still get up every morning at 4:30, go to the plant, do my assembler work, keep the bills paid... I take care of myself just like I always have. The trouble is all centered on what’s happening in my house with him and my things. Outside of that, everything is exactly the same. 

I still drive my '04 Silverado to work every day, for instance. Great truck. I do all the maintenance on it myself. Oil changes every three thousand miles, and I use conventional oil, none of that synthetic stuff they try to upsell you on at those quick-lube places. You go in there for a basic oil change and some kid pulls out your cabin air filter, points to a couple of dry leaves on it, and acts like it's a national emergency. "Sir, you really need to replace this today." I tell them, I can buy that exact filter at AutoZone for twelve bucks and pop it in behind the glovebox myself in two minutes. It's a total scam, how they prey on people who don't know any better. 

My wife took her sedan in once—this was a few years ago—and they charged her eighty dollars for wiper blades. Eighty dollars! I about hit the roof when I saw the receipt. You can get a pair of Rain-X blades for twenty-five bucks and snap 'em on right there in the Walmart parking lot. Takes thirty seconds if you know how the little J-hook works. But yeah, as far as my day-to-day goes, work and all that, I'm doing just fine. It's just the situation at the house that's the issue.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre delusion (persecutory belief that his wife's relative is deliberately moving his tools and sabotaging his fishing plans to force him out of his home) persisting for approximately 9 months. There are no hallucinations (auditory or visual), no disorganized speech (despite tangential, detail-oriented conversational style consistent with premorbid personality/interests, not formal thought disorder), and no negative symptoms. Mood is not notably elevated or depressed, and there is no substance use or medical/neurological cause identified. Functioning at work, self-care, and daily routine (waking at 4:30am, maintaining job performance, managing finances, vehicle maintenance) remains fully intact except for the circumscribed area of belief regarding the relative. This pattern—an isolated, non-bizarre delusional system with preserved functioning and absence of other psychotic or mood symptoms for greater than 1 month—is classic for Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia (F20.9), which requires broader symptom criteria (hallucinations, disorganization, negative symptoms) or functional decline, or F28 (Other psychotic disorder), which would be less specific.
